item.research_question: How can high-entropy alloys be rationally designed and structurally regulated at the (sub-)nanoscale to overcome the limitations of traditional alloys in optimizing electronic structures and maximizing electrocatalytic activity?
item.material_system: High-entropy alloys (HEAs) containing five or more dominant elements (e.g., Pt, Pd, Ni, Co, Fe, Au, Cu, Sn, Rh, Ir, Mo, Ru, Ag, La, Ce, In, Sr, Mn, Al, Ti, Bi, Zn); High-entropy single atoms (HESACs); High-entropy metallic glasses (HEMGs); High-entropy intermetallics (HEIs)
item.processing_route: Thermodynamically nonequilibrium synthesis methods including carbothermal shock (heating to 2000 K for 55 ms with cooling in milliseconds), laser scanning ablation (5 ns pulse duration), and light-assisted flash-thermal shock (1800°C within 5 ms); Wet-chemical co-reduction using metal acetylacetonates; Sequential reduction strategies; Template-assisted synthesis using Al-rich nanowires, Ag nanowires, or PS/PMMA beads; Electrochemical synthesis via nanodroplet-mediated electrodeposition (100-ms electroshock); Melt-spinning followed by electrochemical dealloying
item.test_conditions: Electrocatalytic reactions including oxygen reduction reaction (ORR), hydrogen evolution reaction (HER), oxygen evolution reaction (OER), and CO2 reduction reaction (CO2RR); Operando X-ray absorption spectroscopy (XAS) at applied voltages such as -0.01 V
key_findings: HEA nanoparticles with a particle size of ~3.4 nm were made through a wet-chemical method, and decreasing the size to 1.32 nm was achieved by chemical co-reduction and continuous-flow liquid-phase reduction methods.
Five kinds of metal atoms were incorporated into nitrogen-doped carbon to achieve the atomization of high-entropy concepts, forming high-entropy single atoms (HESACs) with up to 11 metals.
PtRhMoIrCoRuFeNiMnCr ultrathin nanowires were synthesized with an average diameter of ~1 nm using a sequential reduction mechanism regulated by Mo(CO)6.
Ag nanowires served as templates to construct 2D HEA subnanometer ribbons with a thickness of ~0.8 nm, the thinnest among HEAs so far.
Rh sites in RhPtFeCoNi HEA nanoparticles exhibited a negative shift toward lower energy compared with other elements at -0.01 V, serving as electron acceptors.
The intensity of Pt in XANES declined sharply at -0.01 V, indicating that the main active sites in RhPtFeCoNi HEA nanoparticles are Rh and Pt.
A HEA nanoparticle library containing up to eight dissimilar elements (Pt, Pd, Ni, Co, Fe, Au, Cu, and Sn) was built using the carbothermal shock method.
HEA nanoparticles containing up to nine elements (Pt, Ir, Fe, Ni, Co, La, Ce, In, and Sr) were successfully synthesized via millisecond-scale light-assisted flash-thermal shock.
item.mechanism: High mixing entropy reduces the free energy of the solid-solution phase, promoting the formation of single-phase structures and continuous regulation of compositions to optimize adsorption/desorption energies. Lattice distortion creates thermodynamically nonequilibrium states with higher potential energy, reducing energy barriers for catalytic reactions. The cocktail effect generates synergistic interactions between multiple components that produce unpredictable and enhanced catalytic performance. Nanoscale size maximizes surface-active atoms, while anisotropic morphologies provide more exposed low-coordinated atoms and improved mass/electron transport. Amorphous structures (HEMGs) offer abundant surface defects and dangling bonds, while ordered structures (HEIs) provide specific atomic stoichiometry.
item.limitations: Conventional high-temperature/shock-cooling techniques make it difficult to maintain the unique anisotropic structures of nanomaterials. The limitations of selected supports acting as electric conductive and heating elements exist in carbothermal shock methods. Expensive and complex instruments, as well as harsh preparation conditions, make some shock-type strategies impossible to spread widely. Strongly immiscible elements are difficult to alloy in wet-chemical methods, which can induce phase separation and heterogeneity. Metals tend to form Wulff polyhedrons to minimize surface energy, making it difficult for intrinsically nonlayered metals and HEAs to spontaneously form anisotropic structures.
item.future_work: Develop more sophisticated HEA-based nanocatalysts with high-entropy subnanoclusters or single atoms using more advanced methods. Construct a more feasible structure-performance relationship to guide advanced design of HEAs in electrocatalytic future. Explore the interconversion between HEMGs and HEIs under specific conditions such as temperature, stoichiometry, and atom binding environment.
quotes: High-entropy alloys (HEAs) overcome this limitation by manageably tuning the adsorption/desorption energies of reaction intermediates.
The marriage of nanotechnology and HEAs has made considerable progresses for renewable energy technologies, showing two important trends of size diminishment and multidimensionality.

Continuous adjustment of component distribution makes it possible to break the barrier of traditional binary or ternary alloys, providing adsorption/desorption energy toward reaction intermediates closer to the optimal value.

item.research_question: How can the synthesis challenges of high-entropy intermetallics (HEIs) be overcome to create well-defined, structurally ordered nanocrystals with long-range order for electrocatalysis?
item.material_system: (PtIr)(FeCoCu) HEI nanoparticles, (PtRh)(BiSnSb) HEI nanoplates, Pt28Mo6Pd28Rh27Ni15 nanocrystals, PtNiFeCoCu HEA nanoparticles, NiCoFePtRh HEA nanoparticles, ZnNiCoIrMn HEAs, FeCoNiCuMn HEA nanoparticles, IrPdPtRhRu HEA nanoparticles, sub–3 nm HEAs, PtPdIrRuAg HEA nanoribbons, PtIrFeCoNi HEI nanoparticles, PdNiRuIrRh HEA nanoparticles, PtRuNiCoFeMo HEA nanowires, PtRhBiSnSb HEI nanoplates, PtNiFeCoCu HEA nanoparticles, PtBiPbNiCo HEA core/shell nanoplates, CoCuGaNiZn HEAs, AgAuCuPdPt HEAs, AuAgPtPdCu HEA nanoparticles, PdCuAuAgBiIn HEAAs
item.processing_route: Carbon supports preadded to metal precursors followed by annealing at 850°C; complexing-reducing-ordering growth mechanism using preformed Bi-complex nanoplate templates; dealloying with Zn elements as sacrificial metals; anchoring-carbonization strategy for sub–3 nm HEAs; synthesis of ultrasmall nanoparticles and nanowires; formation of core/shell structures with medium-entropy core/high-entropy atomic layer shells
item.test_conditions: 1.0 M KOH electrolyte for HER; 0.5 M H2SO4 containing 0.5 M formic acid for FAOR; 0.1 M KOH solutions for HOR; various potentials versus reversible hydrogen electrode (RHE) for CO2RR; 100-hour HER stability tests; 1000 MOR cycles; practical H2/O2 fuel cells; alkaline electrolytes for ORR and HOR
key_findings: Pt28Mo6Pd28Rh27Ni15 nanocrystals displayed the lowest overpotential of 9.7 mV at 10 mA cm−2 in 1.0 M KOH electrolyte.
Well-dispersed PtNiFeCoCu HEA nanoparticles showed a high mass activity of 10.96 A mg−1Pt at −0.07 V versus RHE toward HER.
Ultrasmall NiCoFePtRh HEA nanoparticles exhibited a low overpotential of 27 mV at 10 mA cm−2 and an ultrahigh mass activity of 28.3 A mg−1 at −0.05 V versus RHE.
ZnNiCoIrMn HEAs exhibited a low OER overpotential of 237 mV at 10 mA cm−2.
Sub–3 nm HEAs anchored on ordered mesoporous carbon showed an electrochemically active surface area (ECSA) of 102.3 m2 g−1, 1.62 times higher than commercial Pt/C.
PtPdIrRuAg HEA nanoribbons showed 21.0 times higher mass activity than commercial Pt/C in alkaline electrolytes.
PtIrFeCoNi HEI nanoparticles achieved an ultrahigh peak power density of 1.73 W cm−2 in practical fuel cells.
PtRuNiCoFeMo HEA nanowires showed a HOR mass activity of 6.75 A mgPt+Ru−1, 19.8 times higher than commercial Pt/C.
PtBiPbNiCo HEA core/shell nanoplates displayed a mass activity of 7.1 A mgPt−1 and a power density of 321.2 mW cm−2 in DFAFCs.
AuAgPtPdCu HEA nanoparticles showed a high Faraday efficiency of 100% at 0.3 V versus RHE toward gaseous hydrocarbons in CO2RR.
PdCuAuAgBiIn HEAAs achieved 98.1% Faraday efficiency toward HCOOH at −1.1 V versus RHE.
item.mechanism: The authors argue that the continuous adjustment of surface electronic structures through high-entropy effects, site-to-site electron transfer, and strong orbital couplings allows for the breaking of linear scaling relationships. This optimization of adsorption/desorption behavior for reaction intermediates (H*, O*, OH*, COOH*, etc.) is achieved by the diverse composition and structure of HEAs, where specific elements act as electron reservoirs, depletion centers, or oxophilic sites to lower energy barriers and stabilize intermediates.
item.limitations: The synthesis difficulty from high-temperature annealing to overcoming the energy barrier from disorder to order makes HEIs a 'benchwarmer'; harsh preparation conditions challenge morphological control; the controllable morphologies of HEAs are very limited; differences in reduction potentials and miscibility behavior add difficulties to fine structural regulations; the complexity of surface and internal structure challenges the identification of active sites; the development is still in its infancy and too early for practical industrial applications.
item.future_work: Developing more controllable synthetic approaches; extending HEAs to other electrocatalytic applications like organic electrosynthesis; leveraging advanced characterizations and in situ spectroscopy to understand the relationship between structure and catalytic activity; addressing scalability, economic feasibility, reproducibility, controllability, and sustainability for industrial integration.
quotes: The agglomeration of nanoparticles was prevented due to the tight interaction between nanoparticles and carbon supports.
The development of these methods provides an effective and feasible strategy for realizing the atomic long-range ordered HEIs.
The continuous adjustment of surface electronic structure is the most typical characteristic of HEAs, which potentially enables the break of scaling relationship in electrocatalysis.
